steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for a theory paper on the expressive power of DeepSets-style set architectures, showing that a bottleneck width polynomial in the set size and feature dimension suffices for high-dimensional features. Cover background on invariant architectures, the open question from prior work, and our contributions.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- Invariant architectures and set functions
- DeepSets and the bottleneck dimension question
- Known results for one-dimensional features
- The open problem for high-dimensional features
- Our contribution: polynomial bounds on L
- Implications: DeepSets vs. Relational Network and practical settings

  - most works use multi-symmetric polynomials (cite) to approximate permutation invariant functions (cite)

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Enforcing invariance in neural network architectures is now a widely used principle for designing deep learning models. In particular, when the task is to learn a function that takes a set as input, the architecture enforces permutation invariance, which means the output should not change when the elements of the input set are permuted. Neural networks that learn set functions have been used in many applications, like particle physics, computer vision and population statistics. Recently they have also become a fundamental module, namely the aggregation operation of neighbors' features in a graph, in graph neural networks (GNNs), which have even broader applications.

Previous works studied the expressive power of neural network architectures for representing set functions. Formally, a set with N elements can be represented as \mathcal{S}=\{{\bm{x}}^{(1)},\cdots,{\bm{x}}^{(N)}\} where {\bm{x}}^{(i)} is in a feature space \mathcal{X}, typically \mathcal{X}=\real^{D}. To represent a set function that takes \mathcal{S} and outputs a real value, the most widely used architecture is DeepSets, which follows Eq. 1.

DeepSets encodes every set element separately via \phi, and after sum pooling it maps the encoded vectors to the output via \rho. Because \phi and \rho are continuous, they can be approximated well by fully-connected neural networks, which matters in practice. DeepSets enforces permutation invariance because of the sum pooling: shuffling the order of {\bm{x}}^{(i)} does not change the output. But the sum pooling compresses the whole set into an L -dimension vector, so there is an information bottleneck in the middle of the architecture. So a core question when using DeepSets to represent set functions is: given the input feature dimension D and the set size N, what is the minimal L needed so that the architecture Eq. 1 can represent/universally approximate any continuous set functions? Many previous works paid attention to this question and it is also the focus of this work.

For the case with one-dimensional features (D=1) there is already an extensive understanding. Zaheer et al. proved that this architecture with bottleneck dimension L=N is enough to accurately represent any continuous set functions when D=1. Later, Wagstaff et al. proved that accurate representations are not possible when L<N, and they further strengthened this to a failure in approximation to arbitrary precision in the infinity norm when L<N.

But for high-dimensional features (D>1), the minimal possible L is still not characterized. Most previous works proposed generating multi-symmetric polynomials to approximate permutation invariant functions. The algebraic basis of multi-symmetric polynomials has size L^{*}={N+D\choose N}-1 (exponential in \min\{D,N\}), so these works by default claim that f in Eq. 1 can approximate any continuous set functions if L\geq L^{*}, and they do not check whether a smaller L is possible. Another work constructed a set function that f requires bottleneck dimension L>N^{-2}\exp(O(\min\{D,\sqrt{N}\})) (still exponential in \min\{D,\sqrt{N}\}) to approximate, but this relies on the condition that \phi,\rho only use complex analytic activation functions. The condition is too strict, since many practical neural networks work on real numbers and even allow non-analytic activations, such as ReLU. So that work left an open question: is the exponential dependence of L on N or D still necessary if \phi,\rho work in the real domain and can use non-analytic activations?

- Our contribution
  - negative answer: first proof that L polynomial in N and D suffices for D>1 (real/complex set functions)
  - two choices of \phi:
    - linear layer + power mapping: N(D+1)\leq L<N^{5}D^{2}
    - linear layer + exponential activation: L\leq N^{4}D^{2}
  - real domain, \rho any continuous function: exact construction, like the D=1 result; other works only approximations
  - \rho as fully-connected net -> universal approximation on bounded input space
  - extensions: permutation-equivariant functions, complex field, same bounds up to constants
- Implications
  - prior work used L gap (complex analytic assumption) to separate DeepSets from Relational Network (pairwise encoding)
  - explains observation that Relational Network does better with smaller L
  - our theory: gap reduces from exponential to polynomial without the strict assumption
  - compute-constrained settings use DeepSets only: GNN aggregation on large networks, hypergraph neural diffusion
  - polynomial L suffices there, but decoder \rho needs non-analytic activations

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Enforcing invariance in neural network architectures is now a widely used principle for designing deep learning models. In particular, when the task is to learn a function that takes a set as input, the architecture enforces permutation invariance, which means the output should not change when the elements of the input set are permuted. Neural networks that learn set functions have been used in many applications, like particle physics, computer vision and population statistics. Recently they have also become a fundamental module, namely the aggregation operation of neighbors' features in a graph, in graph neural networks (GNNs), which have even broader applications.

Previous works studied the expressive power of neural network architectures for representing set functions. Formally, a set with N elements can be represented as \mathcal{S}=\{{\bm{x}}^{(1)},\cdots,{\bm{x}}^{(N)}\} where {\bm{x}}^{(i)} is in a feature space \mathcal{X}, typically \mathcal{X}=\real^{D}. To represent a set function that takes \mathcal{S} and outputs a real value, the most widely used architecture is DeepSets, which follows Eq. 1.

DeepSets encodes every set element separately via \phi, and after sum pooling it maps the encoded vectors to the output via \rho. Because \phi and \rho are continuous, they can be approximated well by fully-connected neural networks, which matters in practice. DeepSets enforces permutation invariance because of the sum pooling: shuffling the order of {\bm{x}}^{(i)} does not change the output. But the sum pooling compresses the whole set into an L -dimension vector, so there is an information bottleneck in the middle of the architecture. So a core question when using DeepSets to represent set functions is: given the input feature dimension D and the set size N, what is the minimal L needed so that the architecture Eq. 1 can represent/universally approximate any continuous set functions? Many previous works paid attention to this question and it is also the focus of this work.

For the case with one-dimensional features (D=1) there is already an extensive understanding. Zaheer et al. proved that this architecture with bottleneck dimension L=N is enough to accurately represent any continuous set functions when D=1. Later, Wagstaff et al. proved that accurate representations are not possible when L<N, and they further strengthened this to a failure in approximation to arbitrary precision in the infinity norm when L<N.

But for high-dimensional features (D>1), the minimal possible L is still not characterized. Most previous works proposed generating multi-symmetric polynomials to approximate permutation invariant functions. The algebraic basis of multi-symmetric polynomials has size L^{*}={N+D\choose N}-1 (exponential in \min\{D,N\}), so these works by default claim that f in Eq. 1 can approximate any continuous set functions if L\geq L^{*}, and they do not check whether a smaller L is possible. Another work constructed a set function that f requires bottleneck dimension L>N^{-2}\exp(O(\min\{D,\sqrt{N}\})) (still exponential in \min\{D,\sqrt{N}\}) to approximate, but this relies on the condition that \phi,\rho only use complex analytic activation functions. The condition is too strict, since many practical neural networks work on real numbers and even allow non-analytic activations, such as ReLU. So that work left an open question: is the exponential dependence of L on N or D still necessary if \phi,\rho work in the real domain and can use non-analytic activations?

Our Contribution. The main contribution of this work is to answer the above question negatively. Specifically, we give the first theoretical justification that L being polynomial in N and D is sufficient for a DeepSets (Eq. 1) like architecture to represent any real/complex continuous set functions with high-dimensional features (D>1). To reduce the gap to practical use, we consider two architectures for implementing \phi (in Eq. 1) and give bounds on L for each:

- \phi adopts a linear layer with power mapping: the minimal L has a lower bound and an upper bound, N(D+1)\leq L<N^{5}D^{2}.

- \phi adopts a linear layer plus an exponential activation function: the minimal L has a tighter upper bound L\leq N^{4}D^{2}.

We start from the real domain and prove that if \rho could be any continuous function, the above two architectures reproduce the precise construction of any set functions for high-dimensional features D>1, similar to the earlier result for D=1. This is different from other works that only present approximating representations. If \rho is a fully-connected neural network, which can approximate any real continuous functions on a bounded input space, then the DeepSets architecture f(\cdot) can approximate any set functions universally on that bounded input space. We also extend our theory to permutation-equivariant functions and to set functions in the complex field, where the minimal L has the same bounds up to some multiplicative constants.

Another comment on our contributions: the same prior work used the difference in the needed dimension L, though with the complex analytic assumption, to show the gap between DeepSets and Relational Network in expressive power, where Relational Network encodes set elements in a pairwise manner instead of separately element by element. This gap explains the empirical observation that Relational Network gets better expressive power with smaller L. Our theory does not contradict this observation, but it shows that without the strict assumption above, the gap can be reduced from an exponential order in N and D to a polynomial order.

Many real-world applications have computation constraints so that only DeepSets and not Relational Network can be used, e.g., the neighbor aggregation operation in GNN applied to large networks, and hypergraph neural diffusion operations in hypergraph neural networks. Our theory points out that in this case it is enough to use polynomial L dimension to embed each element, while the decoder network \rho needs non-analytic activations.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Enforcing invariance in neural network architectures has become a widely used principle for designing deep learning models [1,2,3,4,5,6,7]. In particular, when the task is to learn a function with a set as input, the architecture enforces permutation invariance, which asks the output to be invariant to permutations of the input set elements [8,9]. Neural networks that learn set functions have found a variety of applications in particle physics [10,11], computer vision [12,13] and population statistics [14,15,16], and have recently become a fundamental module (the aggregation operation of neighbors' features in a graph [17,18,19]) in graph neural networks (GNNs) [20,21], which show even broader applications.

Previous works have studied the expressive power of neural network architectures for representing set functions [8,9,22,23,24,25,26]. Formally, a set with N elements can be represented as \mathcal{S}=\{{\bm{x}}^{(1)},\cdots,{\bm{x}}^{(N)}\} where {\bm{x}}^{(i)} is in a feature space \mathcal{X}, typically \mathcal{X}=\real^{D}. To represent a set function that takes \mathcal{S} and outputs a real value, the most widely used architecture, DeepSets [9], follows Eq. 1.

DeepSets encodes each set element individually via \phi, and then maps the encoded vectors after sum pooling to the output via \rho. The continuity of \phi and \rho ensures that they can be well approximated by fully-connected neural networks [27,28], which has practical implications. DeepSets enforces permutation invariance because of the sum pooling, since shuffling the order of {\bm{x}}^{(i)} does not change the output. However, the sum pooling compresses the whole set into an L -dimension vector, which places an information bottleneck in the middle of the architecture. Therefore, a core question in using DeepSets for set function representation is, given the input feature dimension D and the set size N, what minimal L is needed so that the architecture Eq. 1 can represent/universally approximate any continuous set functions. This question has attracted attention in many previous works [9,23,24,25,26] and is the focus of the present work.

An extensive understanding has been achieved for the case of one-dimensional features (D=1). Zaheer et al. [9] proved that this architecture with bottleneck dimension L=N suffices to accurately represent any continuous set functions when D=1. Later, Wagstaff et al. proved that accurate representations cannot be achieved when L<N [23], and further strengthened the statement to a failure in approximation to arbitrary precision in the infinity norm when L<N [24].

However, for high-dimensional features (D>1), a characterization of the minimal possible L is still missing. Most previous works [9,25,29] proposed to generate multi-symmetric polynomials to approximate permutation invariant functions [30]. As the algebraic basis of multi-symmetric polynomials is of size L^{*}={N+D\choose N}-1 [31] (exponential in \min\{D,N\}), these works by default claim that if L\geq L^{*}, f in Eq. 1 can approximate any continuous set functions, but they do not check whether a smaller L is possible. [26] constructed a set function that f requires bottleneck dimension L>N^{-2}\exp(O(\min\{D,\sqrt{N}\})) (still exponential in \min\{D,\sqrt{N}\}) to approximate, but the construction relies on the condition that \phi,\rho only adopt complex analytic activation functions. This condition is overly strict, as many practical neural networks work on real numbers and even allow non-analytic activations, such as ReLU. [26] thus left open the question of whether the exponential dependence of L on N or D is still necessary if \phi,\rho work in the real domain and allow non-analytic activations.

Our Contribution. The main contribution of this work is to give a negative answer to the above question. Specifically, we present the first theoretical justification that L polynomial in N and D is sufficient for a DeepSets (Eq. 1) like architecture to represent any real/complex continuous set functions with high-dimensional features (D>1). To mitigate the gap to practical use, we consider two architectures implementing \phi (in Eq. 1) and specify the bounds on L for each:

- \phi adopts a linear layer with power mapping: the minimal L has a lower bound and an upper bound, N(D+1)\leq L<N^{5}D^{2}.

- \phi adopts a linear layer plus an exponential activation function: the minimal L has a tighter upper bound L\leq N^{4}D^{2}.

We start from the real domain and prove that if the function \rho can be any continuous function, the above two architectures reproduce the precise construction of any set functions for high-dimensional features D>1, akin to the result in [9] for D=1. This contrasts with [25,26], which only present approximating representations. If \rho adopts a fully-connected neural network that can approximate any real continuous function on a bounded input space [27,28], then the DeepSets architecture f(\cdot) can universally approximate any set function on that bounded input space. We extend our theory to permutation-equivariant functions and to set functions in the complex field, where the minimal L shares the same bounds up to multiplicative constants.

A further comment on our contributions: [26] leverage the difference in the needed dimension L, albeit under the complex analytic assumption, to illustrate the gap in expressive power between DeepSets [9] and Relational Network [32], where the latter encodes set elements pairwise rather than separately element by element. This gap explains the empirical observation that Relational Network achieves better expressive power with smaller L [33,23]. Our theory does not contradict this observation, but it shows that without the strict assumption above, the gap can be reduced from an exponential order in N and D to a polynomial order.

Many real-world applications have computation constraints under which only DeepSets, and not Relational Network, can be used, e.g., the neighbor aggregation operation in GNNs applied to large networks [21], and hypergraph neural diffusion operations in hypergraph neural networks [7]. Our theory points out that in this case it is sufficient to use a polynomial L dimension to embed each element, while the decoder network \rho needs to adopt non-analytic activations.
